posts.text:
Today Metaplanet announced that it will issue ¥52bn of zero-coupon Euro-yen convertible bonds due 2031, together with a concurrent share repurchase.

These initiatives are interconnected. The issuance funds the repurchase of our shares at a discount to net asset value, reduces secured borrowing, and releases bitcoin currently pledged as collateral – all with debt that carries no regular interest payments.

I need to limit my comments because, as the bonds are not being offered in the U.S., we are highly constrained in what we can communicate from a regulatory perspective.

But today’s announcement serves an important purpose at this time. Up to ¥28.3 billion of proceeds will be used to repurchase our shares as part of our ¥60bn repurchase program. Up to ¥25.3 billion of this will be executed through an off-auction block trade (ToSTNeT-3) this morning, up to 96,934,800 shares, or 7.1% of shares outstanding, with the balance through market purchases. With our shares trading below the value of our bitcoin holdings, buying them back at these prices captures that discount for shareholders.

Conducting the repurchase concurrently with the bond offering also helps absorb trading activity associated with convertible investors hedging their positions, supporting better pricing for the bonds. Any funds not used during the concurrent repurchase will be applied to subsequent share repurchases or to the repayment of our credit facility.

A further ¥23.6bn will be used to partially repay our credit facility, releasing bitcoin pledged as collateral. This gives us greater financial flexibility to acquire more bitcoin while advancing other strategic initiatives, including our Net Interest Income Strategy.

The initial conversion price is set at a premium to both the current share price and 1.0x mNAV at launch. So, we are buying back shares below the value of our bitcoin holdings, while new shares would only be issued upon conversion at a price above that value.

The bonds are yen-denominated, senior unsecured obligations being placed with international investors that are non-U.S. persons exclusively outside the United States, broadening our investor base. They are supported by our balance sheet and credit rather than specific collateral.

Our total debt will increase, but its composition will improve. Secured, interest-bearing borrowing is replaced with unsecured, non-interest-bearing debt. The result is lower interest costs, a longer tenor on our borrowings, a meaningful repurchase of outstanding shares at a discount, and greater credit capacity to execute our strategic initiatives.

Separately, as announced on August 18, our investment in Super League Enterprise (Nasdaq: SLE) is expected to close shortly, subject to SLE shareholder approval and other closing conditions, after which SLE will be renamed Superplanet, Inc. I will have more to say about that at closing.

For more information, see here the full legal notice in English: https://contents.xj-storage.jp/xcontents/33500/8841083a/4cc3/48ab/9277/945e6a6dae59/140120261013550010.pdf and a presentation deck that describes the issuance and repurchase succinctly: https://contents.xj-storage.jp/xcontents/33500/abcd60ad/8adc/4875/84dd/becc22115456/140120261013550035.pdf

3) Open-weight models are increasingly being post-trained here in America by companies like our portco @FireworksAI_HQ using an enterprise’s private data to create a highly optimized specialized model. This customized model can be combined with a frontier model behind a router to create frontier performance at 40% of the cost to the end customer while consuming the same amount of underlying compute.

Cursor’s Composer, Cognition’s SWE-2, Harvey’s Tenet are all early examples of this. Eventually every large enterprise in the world will likely preserve data sovereignty and post-train their own model using their data. These models will be combined behind a router with 1 or more frontier models. This hybrid, multi-model future has been well articulated by Satya Nadella, Alex Karp and others. “Own your weights, control your future.”
 
It has started to happen: open-weight demand has gone vertical over the last few months in the Vercel and OpenRouter datasets. These specialized open-source models in this hybrid future are just compressing margins at the model layer. And this drives more demand for compute as the compute is effectively being marked up less.
 
Turning to this weekend’s specific controversy. My comments about no one taking unfunded commitments from OpenAI and Anthropic seriously over the weekend were about the $1 trillion plus of “MOUs” signed with various Asian supply chain and semiconductor companies in 2025. No one takes those seriously. Contractual commitments matter and are taken seriously.

Per Anthropic’s leaked S-1, they have committed to spending roughly $11 billion per year with Amazon for the next decade, $15 billion per year with Google for the next 7 years and $5 billion per year with Azure for the next 6 years. These are all priced well below current spot prices for compute *and* current forward prices for compute. The combined $31 billion per year of cloud spending is quite low relative to their reported $70bish ARR given ~80% inference margins and will obviously be internally financed. @altcap doing my best to make you happy and lower the bar. SpaceX has a very different strategy: they sell compute at much higher prices in-line with spot. This may result in an 8-9 month payback which may be close to the financing terms Nvidia has given them. The $161 billion in commitments to Broadcom will require external financing from some combination of Broadcom and private credit, which is beginning to happen. While the headline number of $413 billion of real, actual non-cancellable contracts sounds sensational and scary for Anthropic, it is fairly reasonable when one considers the duration and Anthropic’s scale. We shall have to wait for OpenAI’s S-1 to perform a similar analysis for them.
 
Most of the actual contractual commitments that have been made by OpenAI and Anthropic to various hyperscalers and neoclouds are now well below the current spot price for compute.  This is why Sarah Friar noted that she could sell all of their contracted compute commitments up 3-5x from their contract value. She was speaking the literal truth. In a world where both OpenAI and Anthropic disappeared, their commitments would be quickly assumed at higher prices by a variety of players.  I think the hyperscalers deeply regret *every* contract they signed in 2024, 2025 and perhaps even the first half of this year. As these contracts roll-off and their compute is repriced to market, their revenue growth should steadily accelerate which will help with the funding concerns for AI infrastructure. Result is that I think we may be approaching the peak of external financing as a % of the AI infrastructure buildout (cue at least one widely anticipated $100b hyperscale equity raise and then can put a fork in it).

More to say, but will save it for a later date.

posts.name: Gavin Baker
posts.text:
2) A future where OpenAI and Anthropic are a dominant oligopoly at the model layer is negative for almost every company on earth except the two of them. Especially bad for the entire token supply chain. They would be a monopsony for hyperscalers, neoclouds, and datacenter semiconductors. They would have immense buying power and eventually vertically integrate. Would obviously be terrible for the application layer.  And most importantly terrible for humanity. This is a quasi-consensus opinion in Silicon Valley.
 
This is why fragmentation and competition at the model layer is good for both AI infrastructure and AI applications. The model layer has become dramatically more competitive than it was only 4 months ago with Grok Bot, Muse Wonder and most importantly, open-weight models. I do think people would be shocked by the growth that essentially every open-weight focused inference cloud has experienced since May. This is really good for AI infrastructure demand. 

Noteworthy that even as Anthropic lost share and OpenAI has likely held share, the combination of the two has continued to grow at a really high rate led by OpenAI over the last 3 months. As Eric Vishria noted, everyone can win. As an aside, Muse is going to show us a lot about what matters for share at the frontier: just model dominance on the Pareto frontier or product quality as measured by harness/model integration where I still think Muse Code is behind Claude Code, Grok Build and Codex.  Although it is looking increasingly likely that the model subsumes the harness in the next 18 months.
 
Software had effectively zero marginal costs. AI does not. And therefore open-source impacts traditional software and AI very differently. An Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1, Muse Wonder, GLM 5.3, Kimi K3 token all cost roughly the same amount of compute and energy to produce. Effective per token revenue to the semiconductor industry is *roughly* constant for all these models. However, they charge wildly different prices to end users. An Opus or a ChatGPT token might be marked up 300 to 400% from cost (a 75% to 80% inference gross margin) whereas an open-weight token might only be marked up 50-100% (30-50% inference gross margin).  So for the same $1 in true underlying token cost, an Opus or ChatGPT token generates $4 to $5 in revenue at the model layer where an open-weight token might only generate $2 in revenue at the model layer.  And open-weight models have less buying power than Anthropic and OpenAI so they should generally generate more revenue per token to the clouds and neoclouds than Anthropic and OpenAI.  This is why open-weight models having significant share is the best case scenario for AI infrastructure demand. Robust competition between 4-5 frontier labs that compresses margins is the next best scenario. And ironically, it seems like these cheaper open-weight tokens may be net positive for demand at the absolute frontier of intelligence as we move to agent swarms. Meaning something like “Fable 5.1 extra-high” is worth paying for in a use case where it is coordinating a swarm of 100 open-weight agents.
 
All of this is why compute prices have gone vertical as the model layer became increasingly competitive. Lower margins at the model layer mechanically, even if counter-intuitively, drive more demand for compute. Perhaps the more important dynamic is that as intelligence becomes more economically useful, the value of compute should rise. This was Dwarkesh’s point about an H100 eventually renting out for the annualized value of a software engineer. Seems improbable but I continue to be surprised by the inexorable rise in compute prices. Inference clouds focused on open-weights are allegedly bidding close to ~$100 per watt for Blackwell clusters, which is a massive premium to the $50 per watt Google/SpaceX deal that was widely thought to be at least a local, unsustainable peak in compute pricing. Prices have gone up since that deal per 3P data.

 TLDR: Everyone can win. Open-source, frontier labs, infrastructure, applications and most importantly the American people.
 
I understand all of the jitters about Anthropic losing share, real rates, spreads and second derivatives. Still think the most likely future outcome is a hybrid, multi-model future where almost everyone wins, open-weight tokens are likely the overwhelming majority of tokens, the dominant frontier model companies still do well albeit perhaps not the outcome that seemed possible in May and AI infrastructure/applications benefit immensely from the increased fragmentation, competition and lower margins at the model layer.
 
Lower margins at the model layer mechanically drive higher compute demand as long as someone is willing to pay for the training. And Jensen is obviously willing to be the “trainer of last resort.” As below-market compute contracts signed in 24/25 roll-off and reprice higher, cloud and neocloud revenue should continue to accelerate which will help address financing fears; I think we may be near peak external financing for this buildout. Noteworthy that using data from 3Fourteen Research, B200 clusters will generate a 37% IRR *if* their rental price declines 40% per year. Prices are still going up, but that IRR math is too ridiculous to print. 37% IRRs available at scale should get funded.

Re: this weekends controversy about MOUs, Anthropic’s $413 billion of real contractual commitments sounds scary. Reality is that it works out to roughly $31 billion of annual cloud spend, which is easily internally financed given their reported ARR, and $161 billion of spend at Broadcom which will be financed by Broadcom and private credit.

Continue to believe fragmentation at the model layer is the best outcome for ordinary Americans and humans everywhere. As I have said before, do not trust any 5-20 individuals to make the best possible decisions about the direction of this technology. I want as many AIs as possible to maximize the odds that they encompass the diversity of human values across the world and richness of human variation. And I want an AI that shares my own personal values. Safety, freedom and the maximization of human agency through democratization, distribution and diffusion vs. centralization. History has spoken on the dangers of the latter path.

Finally, from my perspective anything that slows this buildout down is net positive over the long-term as the biggest risk and worst outcome is an *actual* overbuild. We are structurally short watts, wafers and increasingly capital. That is all good. God forbid we were still in ZIRP, TSM ramped capex to 3x their current plan and we weren’t short turbine blades: there would almost certainly be an overbuild and a bubble. That would be terrible. Slower and smoother for longer is better both for investors and for the world. A terrible cyber event is the most plausible near term bear case IMHO, but AI cyberdefense ramping quickly and I was happy to hear Sholto say that cyber probably becomes defense dominant in the near future.

posts.text:
If high-quality bonds protect against one kind of crash but not the other, what else belongs in the portfolio? Many products are sold as crash protection. The fairest test is to see what each did in the two most recent, very different stress years.

The chart repays careful reading.

* Stocks of every kind fell in both years. International stocks and real estate did not protect U.S. investors in either crash. Their case rests on long-run diversification, not crash protection. Within U.S. stocks, value shares held up far better than growth shares in 2022, but not in 2008.

* Long-term Treasuries and commodities are mirror images. Each saved the portfolio in one year and hurt it badly in the other. Holding a modest amount of both is a hedge against not knowing which engine will run.

* Gold roughly held its value in both years. It pays no income, and it can fall sharply in other periods, as it did in the early 1980s and in 2013. It is a store of value in a crisis, not a growth engine. 

*Managed futures gained in both years. These funds follow price trends across stocks, bonds, currencies, and commodities, going long or short. They tend to do well in extended declines of any kind. They can also lag for years in calm, trendless markets, and their fees are higher than index funds’.

*Treasury bills gained in both years. Its cost is low returns in good times.

There are a legion of posters now putting out AI quant trading models. Most are crap.

Here’s a quote from this post: “Betting Against Beta, a classic from every textbook: minus 7.78% a year while the market rose 14.86%. A corpse.”

Of course I can’t find how it’s constructed or what period he’s referring to (or what paper he claims to base this design on).

Welp… There is no period starting from today and looking back any decent amount of time that has BAB significantly down (available on our website). It’s been flattish in the USA for a bit but still good global ex USA. Its long-term record is still great. The chief challenge to BAB comes from Robert Novy-Marx where he says it’s empirically subsumed by the profitablity. This is an interesting debate (we still prefer a portfolio of both, partially as the economic story for BAB is better than the one for profitability). Again, economics not just AI. Economics with AI can be super powerful. AI w/o economics, or any understanding of the literature, in a “small data” problem like investing *at all by high frequencies) is a recipe for silliness. Like the post below.

I suspect what has happened here is a mistake I’ve pointed out in other papers. The BAB factor needs a hedge ratio. You short less than you long as the shorts are (this is the point) much higher beta. If you do it dollar neutral you are running a very short the market position, and not doing the BAB factor as anyone serious has learned in the large literature. Thus in a bull market you wrongly think it stinks.

Or they just did it all wrong in some other way. They don’t explain a lot.

This is why AI in the hands of people who don’t know economics, haven’t read the literature, etc., is handing a nuclear weapon to those who should only have a butter knife if they pass a test and get a license. 

And it’s why I think these people are suppliers not consumers of alpha for the foreseeable future.

One day that may change. Hopefully whoever takes over for me at AQR in my coming dotage (not for a while!) can deal with that.

Oh, and “corpse.” Rude as well as wrong. Cool graphics though.

Jensen Huang promoted it in his first-ever X post. Nearly 200 startups sent a similar letter.

I argued that restricting open models risked removing the incentive for closed-model companies to solve the problem themselves — and could reward negligence by stifling competition while they continued collecting revenue from distillation. The administration did not impose those restrictions.

We are witnessing a historic shift.

The annual spread between the S&P 500's earnings yield and the 10Y Note yield is down to -1.5 percentage points, its lowest since 2009.

Since 2022, this yield difference has fallen -440 basis points, its largest 5-year decline since the 1970s.

As a result, the S&P 500's equity risk premium is on track to post its 3rd consecutive negative annual reading, the longest streak since 2002.

This suggests that, on a yield basis, theoretically less risky 10Y Treasuries are now more attractive than the S&P 500.

In other words, investors are receiving a higher yield from Treasuries than from the S&P 500, despite the additional risk of owning stocks.

Historically, a negative equity risk premium has been associated with strong risk appetite and stretched equity valuations.

We expect an eventful Q4 ahead.
